# Array computations with NumPy

<!--
CHAPTER OUTLINE (draft) — Chapter 4: Array processing with NumPy

Pedagogical arc: In Chapter 3 we computed descriptive statistics "by hand" on
plain Python lists (looping, the `statistics` module). This chapter introduces
NumPy arrays as the standard tool for numerical work: they let us write
element-wise ("vectorized") computations without loops, they are far faster, and
they provide statistical functions directly. We continue with the Bechdel movie
dataset from Chapter 3 so students see the same analyses, now done more cleanly.

Tools assumed so far: base Python (Ch. 2), lists/slicing, the `statistics`
module and Matplotlib (Ch. 3). This chapter ADDS NumPy.
-->

## Introduction: why we need arrays

<!--
- Recall Chapter 3: to find a mean we summed a list in a loop and divided; to
  compute profit per movie we'd loop element-by-element.
- Two problems with lists for data: (1) arithmetic isn't element-wise
  (`list1 + list2` concatenates, `list * 2` repeats), and (2) loops are slow.
- NumPy ("Numerical Python") is the foundation of the scientific Python stack
  (pandas, scikit-learn, etc.). Learn it once, reuse everywhere.
- Set expectations: by the end you can load numeric data into arrays, filter and
  transform it without loops, and compute summary statistics in one line.
-->

## Importing NumPy

<!--
- `import numpy as np` — explain the `as np` convention (used everywhere).
- Re-load the Bechdel data and pull the same lists as in Ch. 3, then convert the
  numeric ones to arrays so the chapter is self-contained.
-->

## Creating arrays

<!--
- From a list: `np.array([...])`.
- Convert the Ch. 3 budget/revenue lists into arrays.
- Creation helpers: `np.zeros`, `np.ones`, `np.arange`, `np.linspace`.
- Note: an array holds ONE data type (unlike a list); contrast with Ch. 2 lists.
-->

## Array attributes

<!--
- `.shape`, `.ndim`, `.size`, `.dtype`.
- 1D arrays (a single variable, e.g. all movie budgets) vs. 2D arrays (a table)
  — keep 2D light; full tables come in the pandas chapter.
-->

## Indexing and slicing

<!--
- Familiar from list slicing (Ch. 2): `arr[0]`, `arr[2:5]`, `arr[-1]`.
- Show it behaves like lists so students transfer prior knowledge.
- Tee up the more powerful boolean indexing below.
-->

## Element-wise (vectorized) operations

<!--
- This is the key idea. `arr * 2`, `arr + arr2`, etc. operate element-by-element.
- Motivating example: `profit = revenue - budget` for ALL movies in one line,
  vs. the loop you'd write with lists. Compare side by side.
- Scalar broadcasting (`arr + 1000000`); briefly name "broadcasting".
- Universal functions: `np.sqrt`, `np.log`, `np.abs`, etc.
-->

## Boolean arrays and filtering

<!--
- Comparisons produce boolean arrays: `budget > 1e8`.
- Boolean indexing to select: `revenue[budget > 1e8]`.
- Counting with `.sum()` on a boolean array (True == 1): e.g. how many movies had
  a budget over $100M? what fraction passed the Bechdel test?
- Combine conditions with `&` and `|` (note parentheses are required).
-->

## Descriptive statistics with NumPy

<!--
- Revisit every statistic from Chapter 3, now as one-liners on arrays:
  `np.mean`, `np.median`, `np.std`, `np.min`, `np.max`, `np.sum`,
  `np.percentile` (quartiles).
- Show these match the `statistics`-module results from Ch. 3 — same numbers,
  less code — to connect the chapters.
- Z-scores in a single vectorized line: `(arr - arr.mean()) / arr.std()`,
  callback to the z-score section of Ch. 3.
-->

## Working across rows and columns (2D arrays)

<!--
- Brief: stack budget & revenue into a 2D array, introduce the `axis` argument
  (`axis=0` down columns, `axis=1` across rows) for aggregations.
- Keep short — a teaser for the data-tables/pandas chapter.
-->

## Summary

<!--
- Arrays vs. lists; vectorization replaces loops; boolean masks for filtering;
  built-in statistics. NumPy is the numeric backbone for the rest of the book.
-->

- Follow Ch. 3's pattern: ::: {.exercise} / ::: {.solution} callout blocks.

### Time series and line plots

Time series data is a sequence of data points recorded over regular time
intervals. A line plot connects data points with straight lines, making trends
and seasonality easy to see. Example: average monthly temperature over a year
(months on x-axis, temperature on y-axis) plotted with
`plt.plot(months, avg_temps, marker='o', linestyle='-', color='red')`.
